_about: Рукописные тексты разделов сайта (13.11.2026): lead - первый абзац под заголовком, body - блок под сеткой. {count} - число моделей раздела, подставляет сборка. Читает scripts/lib/section-texts.mjs.

aircraft.lead: From a folded paper plane to the largest passenger jet ever put into service, this section covers {count} aircraft models. Airliners come in narrow body and widebody types, business jets carry furnished cabins, and helicopters range from air ambulances to utility workhorses. Military transports and fighters, camera drones, long-wing UAVs, a hot air balloon and a row of economy cabin seats complete the list.
body: The airliners are built for close inspection. A generic narrow body jet holds 278,966 polygons and 31 maps at 4096 x 4096. Its paint carries no airline branding, so it stands for commercial aviation without dating the image. A generic widebody reaches 757,593 polygons for its raked wingtips, six-wheel main gear bogies and the panel joins along the fuselage. One narrow body model is built in flight configuration, with the gear retracted and the flaps stowed. A mid fuselage shell cut open at 829,958 polygons serves cabin layout studies, maintenance training and cutaway visuals.

Helicopters keep the features that identify them. An air ambulance helicopter carries its shrouded tail rotor and the clamshell rear doors that take a stretcher, and at 1,248,007 polygons it is unusually heavy for a light twin. A four-blade utility helicopter at 179,287 polygons holds StemCell certification. Military types are modeled for film, games, simulation and museum displays. They include a stealth multirole fighter with faceted intakes and sawtooth panel joints and a high-wing transport with its rear ramp. A long-wing UAV is kept to 39,853 polygons for its V-tail and sensor ball.

Subcategory pages narrow the list to helicopters, fighter jets, airliners, and drones and UAVs, while transports, balloons and cabin interiors stay in the main grid. Rigged aircraft are rare here, so plan on static airframes posed on the ground or in flight. CheckMate Pro certification, which covers real-world scale and clean topology, runs through airliners, helicopters and military types alike. A business jet interior with leather club seats and an open flight deck serves luxury travel scenes, and a folding camera quadcopter comes with its handheld controller.

animals-creatures.lead: Creatures of sea, land and air fill this section: fish and marine animals, butterflies and beetles, wild and farm mammals, birds, pets and fantasy dragons. It also holds natural details on their own, such as sea shells, feathers, a shark jaw and an octopus tentacle, for close-ups without the whole animal.
body: Some animals only make sense in motion, and the rigged models are built for it. A bottlenose dolphin at 11,362 polygons comes rigged, with three maps for the skin, the paler underside and the wet sheen. A green sea turtle is supplied plain and rigged, and its CheckMate Pro topology keeps the shell from deforming when the flippers stroke. A penguin comes with an animation rig for its side-to-side waddle, and a golden hamster with groomed fur plays an idle animation of small sniffs and shifts.

Fur versions keep a light base mesh under the groomed hair, as on a brown bear at 31,471 polygons made for close wildlife shots. A domestic donkey standing square on its hooves follows the same approach at 14,820 polygons. Static animals stay lean so they can be repeated: an elk at 9,229 polygons reads correctly in a valley herd, and an Atlantic salmon at 3,930 is meant for shoals. Insects are judged by surface, so the blue morpho butterfly treats its shifting structural color as a material problem, and the ladybug spends 15 maps on its glossy domed shell.

Dogs, fish and marine animals, birds and insects are gathered on their own subcategory pages, while other mammals, reptiles and dragons remain in the main grid. A golden Chinese dragon in a coiled pose and a winged dragon with folded membrane wings cover fantasy games and film. Smaller pieces suit macro and product work, like a clam shell framing a single pearl or a great white jaw with its replacement tooth rows. A white goose feather needs only 860 polygons and carries StemCell certification. Wildlife films, aquarium and museum exhibits, educational apps and game worlds all find material here.

architecture-landmarks.lead: World landmarks, whole buildings and the small parts of the built environment share this section. It runs from the Eiffel Tower and the Colosseum to a hospital, civic buildings and sports arenas, then down to windows, cinder blocks, pipe fittings, street lamps and signs. Dams, railway track, viaducts and arched brick bridges cover infrastructure scenes.
body: The landmarks are built rather than faked. The Eiffel Tower spends 522,388 polygons on real lattice members instead of cutout planes, so light passes through the trusses as the structure thins toward the top. The Colosseum runs to 1,419,065 polygons and keeps the ruin asymmetric, with standing arcades on one side and the exposed inner structure on the other. An Ionic column carries the fluted shaft and the spiral volutes of its capital, and a classical civic building uses 60 maps for its portico, pediment and cornice runs.

Infrastructure models are made to extend and to sit in terrain. A high speed rail viaduct section at 998,008 polygons tiles end to end into a run of any length, and a straight railway section models its ballast as individual stones. A hydroelectric dam includes spillways, intake towers, a powerhouse and a transmission yard. At building scale, a hospital exterior shows its entrance canopy and ambulance bay. A basketball arena builds every seat in the bowl, so a crowd can be scattered across real seating.

Closer to the ground are the parts a builder handles, such as a plastic window unit with its frame profile and handle. A cinder block has its two voids as real openings, and a PVC pipe kit has elbows, tees and couplers that assemble like real fittings. Many models carry CheckMate Pro certification for real-world scale, so figures, vehicles and terrain sit correctly beside them. Architects, planners, engineering firms, level designers and VR developers use the section for context models, explainers and complete environments.

characters-people.lead: People at work, at play and in uniform make up this section. It covers surgeons, field workers, pilots, chefs and beekeepers, athletes in full gear, a ceremonial guard and figures in sci-fi suits. Robots form a group of their own, from friendly humanoids to warehouse machines, and rigged figures sit beside static posed ones.
body: Working figures carry the gear that identifies the job. A rigged oil and gas field worker wears flame-resistant coveralls with reflective stripes, a hard hat and boots with modeled treads, all within 52,090 polygons. A beekeeper in a white suit with a mesh veil is rigged to lift frames out of a hive. A male surgeon in scrubs keeps a realistic face and gloved hands at 17,689 polygons. A fighter pilot comes with G-suit bladders, harness straps and an oxygen mask with its hose.

Sports scenes have figures of their own. A road cyclist in a red skinsuit rides a racing bicycle mid-pedal, and an American football player wears shoulder pads, cleats and a cage-faced helmet. A mixed martial arts fighter celebrates with raised arms, rigged and with groomed hair. A royal sentry in a scarlet tunic and tall bearskin cap stands to attention at 115,506 polygons. For anatomy courses and fitness media, a full male muscular system separates superficial muscles, tendons and ligaments across 185,778 polygons.

Robots and suits cover science fiction and technology stories. A friendly humanoid with a glossy white shell and a dark visor face holds 75,196 polygons, and a warehouse humanoid has knees that bend backward like a bird's. A squat orange robot slides under shelving pods and carries them to a human picker. A black pressure suit with armored plates and a life-support pack stays light at 17,035 polygons. Medical and industrial training, sports graphics, animation, games and safety explainers are typical uses for these figures.

clothing-accessories.lead: Hats, eyewear, leather goods and footwear sit here beside workwear, spacesuits and a coronation crown. Character artists use the section to dress figures, and product artists use it for single items on a clean background. Expect caps and fedoras, sunglasses and wire glasses, wallets and cosmetic bags, safety jackets, masks and small garment parts such as zippers.
body: Headwear shows how much shape decides style. A fedora keeps 9,100 polygons in quads for the pinched crown, the center dent and the snap brim, the creases that stop it from turning into a trilby. A gray trucker cap builds its brim, foam front and mesh back as separate parts, and a curved-brim baseball cap is light enough to repeat across a stadium crowd. A round pair of wire-frame glasses models the hinges and bridge as real geometry, since a flat plane would vanish edge-on.

Small leather goods rely on texture, so a bifold wallet at 7,455 polygons carries five very large maps for the grain. A leather cosmetic pouch keeps the gentle bulge of a filled bag. A foam clog cuts its ventilation holes as real openings, and an athletic sneaker spends 48,118 polygons on stitched panels, laces and the midsole profile. St Edward's Crown builds its arches, jewel settings and pearl rows as separate geometry across 324,811 polygons, because cameras come close enough to count the stones.

Space history has its own corner: spacesuits of the design worn on the lunar landings, and a rigged extravehicular suit with a gold visor and segmented joints. Work and safety pieces include a high visibility jacket with reflective bands placed by standard and a headband magnifier for jewelers and technicians. A coil zipper is modeled tooth by tooth for macro shots. Fashion e-commerce, costume design, game wardrobes and museum displays all use these pieces, and many pages carry CheckMate Pro certification.

collections-sets.lead: Listings in this section deliver several matching models as one product. Sets cover fruit in whole and cut pieces, cocktail glasses and coffee cups, billboard formats, conveyor and pipework kits, themed historical scenes and anatomy series. Pieces within a set are made to agree in scale and finish, so they combine into one scene without adjustment.
body: The point of a set is that its parts agree with each other. A lime collection supplies whole fruit, halves and wedges, so a wedge on a glass rim matches the fruit beside it in size and skin. A cocktail glass set covers martini, coupe, highball, rocks and flute shapes with matching wall thickness and stem proportions. A coffee cup range pairs takeaway cups and lids with ceramic mugs, espresso cups and saucers, and a cherry set keeps the joined pairs that make the fruit recognizable.

Modular kits follow the way real installations are assembled. Roller conveyor modules come as straight runs, curves, gravity sections and legs that join at one height. The industrial pipe set provides elbows, tees, reducers, flanges, valves and supports on a shared diameter standard. Other sets pair an exterior with its insides. Wind turbines arrive with a nacelle interior holding the gearbox, generator and yaw drive, and an electric car comes with its bare frame and battery pack for a cutaway.

Themed sets furnish a whole setting at once. An ancient Egyptian set combines a sarcophagus, statues and temple elements into a tomb chamber. An ice age set places hunters in hide clothing beside a woolly mammoth with long fur. Teaching sets include a male skeleton in more than one arrangement, prehistoric stone tools with flaked edges and sliced arteries showing each layer of the vessel wall. An emoji pack carries 276 maps, one flat-color texture per emoji, so a full reaction vocabulary arrives in a single import. Game environments, drinks advertising, plant layouts, museums and classrooms are where a matched set saves the most work.

containers-storage.lead: Port yards and pantry shelves both draw on this section. It holds freight and refrigerated containers, wooden crates, steel drums, roll-off bins, locker banks, sacks and milk churns. Everyday packaging is here too: bottles, jugs, cartons, cans, paper cups and takeaway boxes. Shapes are modeled so that stacks, refraction and close-ups hold up.
body: Freight containers anchor the heavy end. A standard twenty-foot freight container holds 42,248 polygons with corrugated walls, corner castings and locking bars, and five maps carry painted steel, faded stencils and rust along the bottom rail. A refrigerated container adds the machinery unit with its grille and fan, the control panel and the air vents. A large open-top roll-off bin with reinforced side ribs suits construction and demolition sites, and a two-row bank of commercial lockers models every door, hinge, latch and number plate.

Packaging is modeled where the light catches it. A PET water bottle keeps its ribs as geometry, because ribs catch light in bands and a smooth cylinder never reads as plastic. A one-gallon jug builds its hollow molded handle, and a paper drink cup models the rolled rim that holds a highlight all the way around. A slatted fruit crate leaves real gaps so light falls through a stack, and a half-filled canvas sack slumps with modeled folds rather than bump maps.

Boxes and crates have a subcategory page, as do barrels and drums, while bottles, cans, cartons and bins stay in the main grid. Lighter props are meant for repetition: a group of rusty waste oil drums at 2,099 polygons can be stacked by the dozen in a scrapyard. Folded paper food trays with a red checker print fill a fairground stand or a food court counter. Logistics visualization, packaging mockups, retail scenes, games and film sets are the usual destinations for these models.

electronics-gadgets.lead: Phones, tablets, laptops and cameras fill much of this section, joined by televisions, server racks, graphics cards, charging cables, handheld radios and travel adapters. Retro pieces such as a CRT television, a folding instant camera and a suitcase record player sit beside current devices. Generic unbranded models share the grid with accurate replicas of specific consumer products.
body: Generic devices are the safe choice for client work and backgrounds. An unbranded slab smartphone with a raised camera module stays light at 15,329 polygons, so it can appear in many hands at once. A generic thin laptop shows its keys, hinge and side ports as real shapes, and a leaner one at 21,136 polygons is meant for desk clutter rather than hero close-ups. A server rack in a generic scheme holds 227,722 polygons, and a set of populated cabinets gives a data center row the variation that real rows have.

Detailed product models focus on what identifies each device. A fully disassembled smartphone keeps the display assembly, battery, logic board, camera module, shields and screws as separate objects. They can be laid out flat, exploded along an axis or animated back into the chassis. A 12.9-inch tablet uses subdivision geometry to keep its continuous edge radius clean at any distance. A DSLR body and lens spends 58,619 polygons on the grip, the mode dial and the barrel rings, since cameras are usually shot within half a meter.

Separate pages narrow the choice to smartphones, cameras, laptops and computers, or headphones and audio. A late consumer CRT set with front controls behind a flip-down door dates a room to the years just before flat panels. A desktop 3D printer comes with a printed figurine on its bed, which turns the machine into a story about making things. Product advertising, tech explainers, repair guides, office and living room interiors, and data hall walkthroughs all rely on these models.

food-beverages.lead: Fresh herbs, cut fruit, roast dishes, fast food, bread, desserts and drinks fill this section of {count} food and beverage models. Herbs and leafy greens are built leaf by leaf, cut fruit carries its realism in large textures, and finished dishes and cocktails arrive assembled for menu, packaging and advertising shots.
body: Each model spends its budget where the food is read. A fresh rosemary sprig builds every needle as geometry across 32,128 polygons, and a mint sprig models the quilted pucker of its leaves in the mesh. A carrot does the opposite: a tapered cone of 943 polygons with five maps at 8192 x 8192 for its ridges, rootlets and soil. A tomato pairs 1,366 polygons with ten maps and StemCell certification, so its subsurface glow behaves the same in a real-time engine as in an offline render.

Prepared food is shaped for the table and the counter. A whole roasted turkey, trussed and browned, keeps the tucked wings and the slight collapse of the breast that make it look cooked. A pile of French fries lays individual sticks at the angles fries really fall, and a baguette spends 65,152 polygons on slashes, split ridges and blistered crust. A finished cocktail comes built, with the glass, the layered pour, the ice, the straw and the garnish already sitting together.

Fruit and vegetables, desserts and sweets, and drinks each open as a narrower subcategory page. Among the sweets are an ice cream cone with its waffle grid cut into the geometry, a spiral lollipop and a gingerbread house trimmed with piped icing and candy canes. A single popcorn kernel at 465 polygons is meant for instancing by the thousand, and a separate set shows the kernel unpopped, half open and fully popped. Food advertising, menu boards, recipe apps, packaging mockups and game kitchens are where these models end up.

furniture-interior.lead: Rooms are furnished from this section, from chairs, tables and drapery to refrigerators, laundry machines and bathroom fixtures. Outdoor loungers and grills, airport and home theater seating, and complete interiors ready for dressing are here as well. Pieces range from light background fill for wide shots to dense hero models built for close-ups.
body: Fabric is where polygon count buys realism. A stage curtain spends 229,816 polygons on deep vertical folds that gather on a top rail and pool at the floor. A pair of pleated curtains at 168,766 polygons keeps the gathered heading and the soft break where the fabric meets the floor. A mirror ball builds each square tile as its own flat plane, so it throws real dots of light. A claw vending machine arrives empty, ready to be filled with plush prizes of your own choosing.

Everyday pieces stay as light as their role allows. A close-coupled toilet at 4,844 polygons gets the bowl profile, cistern and seat right without spending on detail a wide shot never resolves. A one-piece monobloc plastic chair stacks without hardware, and a school desk and chair includes the pencil groove and the book shelf under the seat. Airport seating hangs its shells off a shared beam, and a cast iron park bench carries its character in the scrollwork of the end frames.

Chairs, tables, beds, and cabinets and shelving have pages of their own, while appliances, fixtures and full rooms appear in the main grid. French door and side-by-side refrigerators, a white washer and dryer pair and a gas grill with separate grates and side shelves cover the working parts of a home. Complete scenes include an empty bar with counter, stools and lounge seating, and a fully populated computer laboratory at 4,096,036 polygons. Interior design studios, property visualization, event planners and set dressers work with these models.

industrial-equipment.lead: Construction sites, farms, factories and energy projects are the settings for this section. It holds onshore and offshore wind turbines, mobile cranes, boom lifts, piling rigs, tractors and harvesters. Conveyors, pumps, pipelines, electrical panels and scaffolding follow, up to a complete tunnel boring machine. Many pieces are modular or built with separate moving parts.
body: Wind and gas sites can be assembled from these models. A generic offshore turbine stands on a monopile with a yellow transition piece and carries no manufacturer badge. An onshore turbine at 20,879 polygons is light enough to repeat along a ridge. A nacelle interior at 462,736 polygons shows the main shaft, gearbox, generator and yaw drive, the parts that explain how a turbine works. A fracking platform gathers the wellhead, pump units, tanks and manifold piping, and an above-ground gas pipeline runs on steel saddles with flanged joints.

Heavy machinery is built with its working parts separate. An all-terrain mobile crane at 820,533 polygons includes telescopic boom sections, outrigger pads, a counterweight stack and a cab interior, and it comes rigged. An articulating boom lift builds its boom sections as separate parts so it can extend. The tunnel boring machine reaches 4,644,399 polygons with 72 maps, covering the cutterhead with its discs, the shield, the erector arm and the trailing back-up. A scaffold bay models every coupler, and conveyor sections chain into a production line.

Narrower pages exist for cranes, tractors and agriculture, industrial robots, and forklifts and loaders. On the farm side, a generic tractor appears in dirty working condition with a detailed cab, and a large tractor hauls a high-sided tipper trailer. A hay bale spends 977,700 polygons on individual straws at the cut ends. A horizontal SCARA arm for pick-and-place work stands for factory automation. Engineering firms, safety trainers, energy companies and simulation developers use these models in presentations and training.

kitchen-tableware.lead: Place settings, cafe tables and picnic blankets all start here: cutlery, napkins, serving trays and cloches, graters and wooden spoons, party cups, coolers and picnic baskets. The section also gathers home objects that live near the table, such as ceramic vases, folded towels, a seedling tray and cardboard boxes.
body: Table pieces are kept light and clean, since they appear by the dozen. A knife, fork and spoon set at 3,038 polygons gives flatware the matched bowl shapes and handle profiles of one pattern. A silver dessert spoon gets by on 484 polygons because its silhouette is the object, and a wooden spoon at 280 polygons is a clean quad shell. Napkins come two ways: a cotton napkin with modeled cloth thickness, and a fabric one built in triangles to keep a soft draped edge.

Serving pieces carry the harder surfaces. A serving cloche at 36,210 polygons is a mirror-polished dome that reflects the whole room, so its geometry has to be flawless, and it carries StemCell certification. An antique silver tray frames a flat center with a raised decorative border. Outdoor meals get a wicker picnic basket with its weave modeled strand by strand and a checked blanket draped over uneven ground. A red 48-quart cooler comes with its drain plug and swing handle.

A clear plastic party cup at 406 polygons is about as light as a prop gets, made for tables, bins and hands. The rest of the section is a mix of household objects. A box grater shows a different cutting pattern on each face, and an under-sink reverse osmosis system lines up its filter cartridges beside a storage tank. An hourglass timer with turned wooden caps, a glass memorial candle lantern and a leather ring box complete the mix. Restaurant and hospitality visualization, kitchen design, food styling and lifestyle product renders call for exactly these props.

lighting.lead: Light sources from bare bulbs to film studio spotlights gather in this section. It covers incandescent, LED and fluorescent bulbs, desk and floor lamps, lanterns of paper, glass and pierced metal, warning beacons and grow lights for indoor plants. Some bulbs and lanterns are modeled switched on, with a glowing filament or bulb already in place.
body: Bulbs are made for close framing. A classic pear-shaped incandescent bulb at 7,538 polygons keeps the glass envelope smooth, the coiled filament on its supports and the screw base threads crisp. A separate illuminated model gives most of its 7,762 polygons to the glowing coil. A fluorescent tube at 1,936 polygons uses three small maps at 512 x 512, since tubes appear by the dozen and show little surface variation. A large globe filament bulb in vintage style and a compact LED bulb with a flat top suit bare cords and chandeliers.

Lanterns turn the light pattern into the subject. A pierced Moroccan lantern with an onion-dome top gives each star and arch opening real depth across 78,144 polygons, so light spills out in sharp shapes. A round paper lantern over a wire spiral, a red ribbed lantern of the Japanese kind and a sky lantern with a burning fuel cell suit festivals and evening scenes. A brass genie lamp with a long spout and a black wall lantern on a scroll bracket cover the decorative side.

For production scenes there is a film studio fresnel spotlight with barn doors and concentric lens rings at 123,149 polygons. A halogen photo lamp on a tripod and a ring light with a phone holder serve photo and streaming setups. Lamps and light bulbs each have a subcategory page. Household fixtures include a jointed blue desk lamp with a dome shade and a modern floor lamp that splits into three arms. The section serves lighting designers, interior visualizers, film previsualization teams and product artists.

medical-3d-models.lead: Anatomy figures that let a presentation fade from skin to the structures beneath, along with skulls, organ systems and the instruments of a working clinic. The section also reaches into the lab and the pharmacy, with a virus particle, a molecule, syringes, endoscopes, microscopes, pill bottles and hospital beds.
body: The anatomy is built in layers rather than painted on. The Complete Female Body Anatomy holds 784,570 polygons, and each body system is a separate structure with its own material. That lets systems be isolated, made transparent or peeled away one layer at a time. The Male Full Body Anatomy and Skin follows the same idea with 777 texture maps, and its skin sits correctly over everything underneath. For a single region, the Male Arm Full Anatomy and Skin carries skin, muscle, vessels and bone in 51,639 polygons. The Human Cardiovascular System Full Body builds arteries and veins as continuous branching tubes, so the two networks can be colored and labeled separately.

Lighter models cover the rest of a medical scene. The Male Human Skull models the eye sockets, cheekbone arches and jaw hinge directly in 8,954 polygons. The Endoscope fits its angulation wheels, valve ports, insertion tube and distal tip into 6,117 polygons. The Disposable Syringe 2ml Set shows the barrel graduations, plunger seal and needle hub, because a plain barrel reads as a toy. The Hospital Bed 2 builds its deck sections as separate parts, since a hospital bed exists to change shape. The section also edges into science teaching, with an ethane molecule at correct tetrahedral angles and a portable pH meter caught mid-measurement.

Human Anatomy and Skeleton & Bone hold the figures for courseware, patient education and medical animation. Medical Equipment gathers the ward, the lab and the pharmacy, from microscopes to a headwall system with a vital signs monitor and suction unit. Dental is the place for teeth and jaws. The anatomy figures named here carry CheckMate Pro certification, while a coronavirus particle with individually built spike proteins carries StemCell.

military-vehicles.lead: Main battle tanks, tracked and wheeled armored carriers, self-propelled artillery and air defense vehicles, from Cold War designs to recent concepts. Long-range bombers and a small troop helicopter sit alongside them. A few civilian pieces share the section too: armored cash-in-transit trucks and a sidewalk delivery robot.
body: Tanks carry much of the detail here, especially in the tracks and road wheels. A Soviet-designed main battle tank fitted with explosive reactive armor reaches 1,368,860 polygons, covering every armor block, road wheel, track link and hatch. A gas-turbine tank whose silhouette has barely changed through years of upgrades is built in 479,236 polygons with 13 texture maps. Two Cold War French tanks show cast turrets and long guns, and one of them is rigged. A battle-worn light tank has mud caked along its lower hull, and a modular tracked chassis without a turret is ready for a weapon or sensor module.

Infantry and support vehicles fill out the ground force. An eight-wheeled amphibious armored personnel carrier has a water jet at the stern and a hull shaped to float with a squad inside. A tracked infantry fighting vehicle pairs a large gun with an autocannon in its turret. A wheeled self-propelled howitzer in desert camouflage models the spades and stabilizers that mark the change from driving to firing. A rigged military truck can raise its air defense missile canisters, the pose that defines that system in photographs.

In the air, the section holds a Soviet swing-wing supersonic bomber, a long-range bomber with huge contra-rotating propellers and a small helicopter with external troop benches. War films, documentaries, strategy and simulation games, museum displays and training courses all draw on these models. Several, including the self-propelled howitzers and the long-range bomber, carry StemCell certification with standardized PBR materials. The cash-in-transit trucks, with reinforced rear doors and small armored windows, belong in heist films and city traffic instead.

musical-instruments.lead: Concert harps and grand pianos, brass and woodwind, folk instruments, bells and studio microphones. Around them sits the gear of music making: DJ players, turntables, pedal boards, acoustic foam, metronomes and road cases. Keys, valves, strings and controls are modeled as parts, so the instruments hold up in close shots of stages, classrooms and recording rooms.
body: Orchestral instruments are built down to their mechanisms, where most of the polygons go. The pedal harp spends 82,688 polygons on the scrolled crown, the tuning pins and strings that stay straight and evenly spaced. The Bassoon Musical Instrument puts its detail into the silver keys, rods and tone holes along the folded body. The Golden Saxophone models every key cup, rod and pad guard rather than painting them onto the body. A concert grand with its lid raised uses 664,885 polygons for the strings, hammers, pedals and curved rim. The Trumpet shapes its three piston valves and coiled tubing in 17,842 polygons.

Recording and performance gear widens the section beyond the instruments themselves. A professional DJ setup of two media players and a mixer models each jog wheel, fader and cue button. It arrives without texture maps, which leaves the metal, rubber and screens to your own shaders. A direct-drive turntable carries the strobe dots on its platter edge and an S-shaped tonearm. The Recording Studio Interior with Equipment is a whole room of 3,925,292 polygons, with cables, knobs and foam panels modeled rather than painted. A heavy-duty road case on casters covers the touring side.

Older and folk instruments add range, such as a Renaissance lute with a ribbed back and a sharply bent pegbox. A kemence comes with its horsehair bow in 7,255 polygons. The pellet drum has beads on cords that strike both heads when the handle twists. The harp, bassoon, flute and clarinet carry CheckMate Pro certification, which checks scale and topology. The instruments here are static models, so lids, valves and pedals sit in fixed positions for film sets, music videos, product renders and games.

nature-plants.lead: Trees, flowers, leaves, grass, mushrooms and stones for landscapes and still lifes. Next to them sit natural effects that are hard to model: water splashes frozen mid-flight, ice cubes, hailstones and a soap bubble. Some pieces are light building blocks for scattering, and others are heavy trees built for hero shots.
body: The large trees spend their polygons where each species is recognized. The Flowering Cherry Tree is almost all blossom, set in dense clusters along the branches with the branch structure still visible, at 1,630,492 polygons. The Red Oak Old Tree Winter puts 275,063 polygons into bare limbs, since a leafless tree is read entirely through taper and forking. The Green Plum Fruit Tree hangs unripe plums among dense leaves on a gnarled trunk. For games, the Low Poly Pine Trees Set uses layered conical crowns for forests and mountain trails.

Small components are made to be multiplied. The Cherry Leaf is 562 polygons and the Single Acorn 768, both in quads, so thousands can be scattered across an orchard or a forest floor. The Branch With Leaves 2 is meant to hang across a window frame or blur the foreground of a shot. The Centipede Warm Season Grass clump is a source object for lawns, roadsides and golf course roughs. Flowers run from an orchid stem with real petal geometry in 2,358 polygons to a gerbera with dense rings of ray petals for tabletop close-ups.

The splash models carry StemCell certification and stand in for a fluid simulation with a sculpted shape. The Crown Splash builds the beads along its rim, and the Water Splash in Air freezes a ring of liquid with its sheet and breaking droplets. For browsing by subject, the Tree, Flower and Rock & Terrain subcategories narrow the grid. Architects plant sites with these models, environment artists dress game levels, and product teams stage cold drinks with the ice.

other.lead: Objects that belong to no larger category gather here, and they fall into a few clear groups. There are emoji and hand gestures, coins and payment cards, and pens, letters and office supplies. Street litter forms another group, with crumpled newspaper, broken glass and a crushed bottle. A handful of one-off props completes the mix.
body: Small objects seen up close carry the most careful detail. The US Quarter puts its 2,908 polygons into relief, with the portrait, lettering and reeded edge built as real depth. The Classic Fountain Pen models the nib with its breather hole and slit. The Steel Ballpoint Pen keeps the barrel taper, clip and knurled grip in 1,842 polygons. The Open Journal curves its pages toward the spine, with UVs laid out so your own handwriting or diagrams can go on as a texture. The Old Letter is one curled sheet in 508 polygons, with the soft fold lines of reopened paper.

The emoji keep the rounded, stylized look of the flat icons they come from. The Thumbs Up Gesture Emoji turns the glyph into a real hand shape in 625 polygons without losing its instant readability. The Emojis Set gathers glossy smiley faces with hearts and tears for social media clips. The litter group exists to make a street feel lived in. The Newspaper Litter 2 spends its polygons on folds and creases, and the Broken Glass Fragments follow the shapes of real breakage. The Crushed Plastic Bottle has buckled walls, a twisted neck and a collapsed base.

Emoji, Coin & Currency and Stationery & Office each have a page of their own. Beyond those groups the section is genuinely mixed. A woven crown of thorns has individually built thorns, and a roll of duct tape lifts its loose end slightly from the surface. A slender cigar shows the spiral seam of its wrapper, and a flat sports car silhouette serves road signs and parking graphics. When a prop cannot be found in a more specific section, this grid is worth a scroll.

ships.lead: Working vessels, warships and pleasure craft, {count} models in all. Container ships, gas carriers, tankers, barges and push boats sit beside destroyers, cruisers, submarines and an aircraft carrier. Sailing and motor yachts, fishing boats and a traditional dhow cover leisure and heritage. Many hulls come with modeled deck hardware, from mooring winches to standing rigging.
body: Merchant ships are built at hero scale. The Container Ship Generic reaches 5,769,509 polygons, with hatch covers, lashing bridges, cell guides, bridge wings and a deck load of containers that are individual objects. The Gas Carrier Ship is recognized by the pressure domes rising above its deck and carries 40 texture maps. The Flat Top Barge is an open deck with no hold and no sides, textured with 13 maps at 4096 x 4096. A river push boat comes paired with its pontoon barge, squared push knees and raised wheelhouse.

Naval models are built around their silhouettes. A guided missile destroyer from the backbone class of the American fleet carries fixed radar panels, vertical launch cells and a helicopter deck in 1,558,756 polygons. A stealth destroyer with an angular tumblehome hull needs only 77,676 polygons, because flat surfaces stay crisp with few faces. Two submarines show the contrast between a missile boat with a long flat deck behind the sail and a finer attack boat. A Chinese carrier built with catapults shows its launch tracks, elevators and deck markings.

For marinas and coastlines, the Offshore Sailing Yacht 2 builds standing and running rigging as geometry, with 20 maps for gelcoat, teak, sailcloth and stainless fittings. The Fishing Trawler is a subdivision surface, so its hull keeps the sweep at any render resolution. The Qatar Traditional Boat follows the shell-first dhow hull with a raked stem and a single lateen sail. Separate pages for Boat & Yacht, Submarine and Naval Ship sort the fleet by type. Simplified versions of some warships trim fine fittings while keeping the turrets and superstructure.

signage-decor.lead: Decorative objects and set dressing: statues and figurines, party balloons, festive props, origami and trophies. Paper and media items make a room look lived in, from vinyl records, CD jewel cases and film rolls to magazine piles and rolled house blueprints. A graduation cap and an empty snow globe sit among them as well.
body: Monuments form a distinct group. The Statue of Liberty without Pedestal is sculpted in 575,096 polygons, dense enough for a close camera pass along the robe folds, torch, tablet and crown. A broken head of the same statue serves ruin and collapse imagery in film and illustration. An open-armed statue on a mountaintop plinth keeps the blocky soapstone tiling of its surface in only 10,550 polygons. A white moai prepared for printing preserves the heavy brow, long nose and carved back designs in a clean solid form.

Celebration props stay light. The Red Balloon with Ribbon is 5,166 polygons, so a full bunch can float over a party table without slowing the scene. The Blue Balloon carries translucent latex, so light passes through it instead of bouncing off a painted sphere. The Paper Boat builds its creases as real edges, and the Graduation Cap with Tassel lets the tassel hang from its button. The Santa Sleigh with curled runners and the Empty Snow Globe both come empty, ready for gifts or a scene of your own.

Figurines round out the section, from a beckoning cat with a raised paw and bell to a jade statue of the Egyptian cat goddess. An award mask trophy gets its whole effect from the cast metal rather than from fine detail. A CD jewel case models its hub teeth and hinge pins, and the vinyl record carries the groove band and center label. These pieces dress interiors, retail windows, holiday campaigns, period sets and game levels.

space-scifi.lead: The section sets {count} models of real and invented spacecraft side by side. Satellites, a space telescope, probes, launch vehicles, a lunar rover and a Mars lander share the grid with flying saucers, a dropship and a retro hovercar. A few earthbound pieces, such as an antique globe and a moon lamp, suit classrooms and interiors.
body: The real hardware is modeled around the details that specialists check first. A GPS satellite carries its solar array panels, the antenna farm on the earth-facing deck and the thruster nozzles in 72,381 polygons. The orbiting space telescope has its aperture door, high-gain antennas and the handrails astronauts used on servicing missions, with 26 maps at 4096 x 4096. The lunar rover from the crewed moon missions builds its wheels from woven wire mesh with chevron treads, and its maps include the dust that coated everything.

Launch vehicles cover old and new spaceflight. A reusable booster comes down tail first on spread landing legs, with grid fins and a scorched body across 537,374 polygons. The moon rocket with white stages, a black roll pattern and an escape tower reaches 3,237,563 polygons. A deep space probe spends its budget on the ribbed high gain dish, the magnetometer boom and the thermal blanket folds over the bus. A Mars lander shows its round solar arrays deployed beside the seismometer dome.

On the fiction side, the Alien UFO is a classic flying saucer in clean quads with a domed cockpit and panel seams around the rim. The Sci-Fi Dropship Landing Position rests on its struts at 1,886,507 polygons, and the Red Hovercar Old is a rigged retro flying car on hover pods. Documentaries, news graphics, science lessons, films and game environments all use this kind of hardware, and the Earth Stylized with Mask was made for pandemic explainers.

sports-recreation.lead: Balls, rackets, clubs, helmets, gloves, goals and hoops for team and individual sports, plus fitness, camping and climbing gear. Nets, strings and stitching are modeled as geometry where a close shot needs them, which matters for broadcast graphics, advertising, retail imagery and sports games.
body: Each ball is built around the feature that defines it. The Golf Ball Generic carries its dimple pattern in 31,980 polygons, all quads, in an unbranded form. The Baseball Ball 2 keeps the raised seams that let a thrown ball curve. Nets get the same care, and the Soccer Goal hangs its net with the right sag. The Basketball Hoop builds its net from cord geometry, along with the backboard, breakaway rim and mounting arms.

Equipment follows the same logic. A tennis racquet spends most of its 45,077 polygons on a string bed of real crossing geometry, so it casts the right shadow. An American football helmet models the facemask bars, shell vents, chin strap and interior padding. The Boxing Gloves are shaped with the thumb wrapped and the knuckle padding full, while a pair of MMA fight gloves has real finger openings. The 2 Iron Golf Club keeps its loft angle, hosel bend and grooved face in 2,274 polygons.

For trails and campsites, the Folded Sleeping Bag shows compression straps biting into the rolled fabric. The Rock Climbing Rope is a properly flaked and tied coil, and the Vintage Camping Tent Set pitches canvas ridge tents with guy ropes and wooden pegs. Ball, Hockey, Fitness & Gym and Camping & Outdoor each open as a narrower page. The section also reaches surfboards, padded wrist and ankle weights, self-balancing hovershoes, a greyhound starting trap, a dog agility bridge and a runner caught mid-stride.

tools.lead: Hand and power tools, workshop and garage equipment, and the hardware around them: drills, caulking guns, tongs, ladders, ratchet straps, wire rope, paint cans and welding helmets. The section's {count} models also cover shops and public spaces, with a shopping cart, a CCTV camera, a tire air station and a shoe sole cleaner.
body: Several tools are built from separate parts that move. The Cordless Drill has a keyless chuck, clutch collar and trigger, and its battery pack can come off on camera. The Two Post Lift swings its arms out to match whatever vehicle parks between the columns. The Legal Scales keep column, beam, chains and pans apart, so the beam can tip to one side. The Silicone Sealant Pistol with Tube shows a toothed plunger rod and a cut nozzle with dried sealant around the tip.

Other models earn their detail in surface and material. The Steel Wire Rope builds the helical strand pattern into 2,432 polygons, since that spiral catches light in bands. The Old Key is a small object meant for macro shots, with 19 maps for casting flash, tarnish and wear on the bit. The Shopping Trolley builds its cart basket from real wire geometry, which throws a lattice shadow on the floor. The Thermal Imaging Camera gives its germanium lens the flat dark look of real thermal optics.

Garages, workshops, construction sites and store shelves are the usual settings for these models, along with product renders, industrial visualization and safety training. The Welding Mask models its flip-up filter frame, dark lens and adjustable headgear, and the drill, the lift and the scales carry CheckMate Pro certification. The Mining Drill Bit, a tricone bit with carbide buttons, and the Single Sided Wooden Ladder carry StemCell certification.

toys-games.lead: Nursery toys next to the props of game tables and casinos. Teddy bears, wooden alphabet blocks, nesting dolls, puppets and pool floats share the section with dice, poker chips, playing cards, slot machines and a twisting puzzle cube. The models suit animation, advertising, board game and casino visuals, and children's learning material.
body: Table and casino props are built to survive close-ups and to look right in quantity. The 6 Edged Dice cuts its pips in as real geometry with radiused corners, so a rim light does not flatten them. The Blank Poker Chip leaves its inlay flat for a client's design, and the Poker Chips Set arrives in stacks and loose pieces. The Full Deck of Playing Cards models all fifty-two cards as separate planes that can be fanned, stacked or dealt. The Casino Slot Machine Generic is unbranded, so the cabinet can carry your own artwork.

Classic toys are split into separate parts wherever a real one comes apart. Every block in the Alphabet Wooden Blocks is its own object with worn edges and modeled letters. The twisting puzzle cube builds each cubie separately, so a layer can turn and show the puzzle mid-solve. The Matryoshka Doll Set gives the full progression of sizes from one turned profile. The Teddy Bear keeps the muzzle seam and ear cups crisp at 21,251 polygons, and the unicorn pool float shows the seam welds of a hand-sealed toy.

Characters and learning toys bring a softer, more playful style to the section. A wooden puppet boy waves hello, and a hand puppet opens its mouth in surprise. A children's toy food set is light enough to scatter across a playroom floor. A set of plastic geometric solids serves classroom lessons on shapes and volume. A polyhedral dice set for tabletop role-playing carries 30 maps for translucent color and printed numbers. A blocky pixel-style bow and arrow builds its voxel steps as real geometry rather than smooth curves.

vehicles.lead: Cars, pickups, vans and box trucks, semi trucks with trailers, buses and motorcycles, plus the trains, airport carts, wheels, tires and charging posts that surround traffic. Recognizable production vehicles sit next to unbranded generic designs for scenes that must not show a badge.
body: Passenger cars are modeled to the proportions that make them recognizable at a distance. A sedan with a low nose and no grille, a single unbroken roof glass and flush door handles is built in 116,225 polygons with nine texture maps. A mid-size sedan with a simplified interior keeps its detail on the exterior, where most scenes need it. The Generic Hybrid Car serves advertising, architectural visualization, training material and games that want a contemporary car without anyone's badge. A modern black coupe shows its surfacing through reflections that run unbroken down the flank.

Commercial vehicles cover city streets and highways. The Semi Truck with Trailer Generic Simple Interior models the fifth wheel, air lines, fuel tanks, mudflaps and ribbed box trailer in 724,720 polygons. A cab-over box truck adds a roller door, and a classic split-windshield van rebuilds its V-shaped nose, roof gutters and chrome bumpers. Rail has its place too, with a high-speed trainset at 3,960,288 polygons and a diesel locomotive paired with a covered hopper car. Both are detailed for a camera traveling along the body.

Smaller pieces fill a garage or showroom, from wheel and tire assemblies to an open-wheel racing wheel with a slick tire. A road bike builds its spokes and drivetrain as geometry, and an EV charging post has a cable that hangs and coils. Truck, Trailer, SUV, Bus and Motorcycle are listed as subcategories for browsing by body type. Military logistics appears too, with a palletized load system truck, a heavy equipment transporter and an amphibious scout car.

weapons.lead: Historical and modern arms as props and reference objects: swords, knives and arrows, rifles and revolvers, missiles and launchers. Protective gear goes with them, from aircrew helmets and holsters to body armor. The models are made for film and television, games, simulation, museum displays and educational material.
body: Blades and historical pieces are modeled for close inspection. The Katana Sword shapes the gently curved single-edged blade, the round guard and the diamond pattern of the grip wrap in 13,132 polygons. The Viking Arrow needs only 632 polygons, with its maps laid out in a long narrow shape that matches the object. The Old Cannonballs have pitted, uneven surfaces rather than true spheres, and a short-handled war hammer from Norse myth carries carved knotwork and engraved runes. A pocket multi-tool knife holds its blade, scissors, nail file and tweezers in their slots.

Firearms and missiles are built for the camera. A classic assault rifle with a curved magazine and wooden stock keeps its receiver, sights and magazine ribs sharp in 37,364 polygons. A Western gun belt pairs tooled leather and cartridge loops with a revolver in a low-slung holster. Larger systems range from a sea-skimming anti-ship missile with cruciform wings to a truck-mounted launcher in desert camouflage and a mobile missile defense battery with its radar.

Protective gear sits beside the arms. A helicopter aircrew helmet carries the boom microphone that sets it apart from a fixed-wing helmet. A plate carrier vest comes with a ballistic helmet, pouches and webbing. A naval rotor cipher machine in its wooden case, with keyboard, lampboard and plugboard exposed, belongs with the historical pieces. The Rifle, Pistol, Missile & Rocket and Knife & Sword subcategories group the arms by type for period films, game levels and museum reconstructions.

aircraft/helicopters.lead: Helicopters in every working role: small two-seat machines, corporate and offshore twins, air ambulances, rescue and police types, military utility and attack helicopters, and a few concept designs. Besides complete airframes, the section holds cockpits, control sticks and instrument panels. Some scenes place a helicopter on a ship deck or inside a field shelter.
body: The detail follows the job each machine does. A twin-engine military utility helicopter at 332,047 polygons keeps the door tracks, the refueling probe fitting, the exhaust suppressors and the antenna array. Those parts set it apart from a generic airframe. A small two-seat helicopter is mostly exposed structure, so its tube frame, belt drive and rotor head share 87 texture maps. An air ambulance spends 42 maps at 4096 x 4096 on markings, reflective striping and registration numbers. The offshore crew transport keeps its flotation sponsons and rear cargo ramp.

Interiors and controls have pages of their own. The flight deck of a light twin brings glass displays, overhead switch panels, seats and pedals in 515,887 polygons. A cyclic stick of 13,901 polygons builds the trim hat, trigger and radio switch as geometry rather than paint. Larger scenes give helicopters context: a research vessel with one on its aft deck, a deck crane lifting a damaged hull, a forklift loading a tandem-rotor transport.

Many airframes in this corner of the Aircraft category carry CheckMate Pro certification, which means real-world scale. The StemCell models add several formats from one source with PBR materials. Rigged helicopters are rare, so rotors are usually modeled in place for stills and flybys. Film crews, simulator and rescue training teams, game studios and architects placing a rooftop helipad will find their machine here.

aircraft/fighter-jets.lead: Fighter aircraft from the propeller era to stealth designs: Second World War piston fighters, the first swept-wing jets, Cold War interceptors, modern multirole and carrier fighters, and experimental demonstrators. The section also holds cockpits, an afterburning engine and pilot figures signaling from the canopy, plus simplified airframes in flight poses for distant shots.
body: Silhouette carries a fighter, and the models here are built around it. A British wartime fighter with elliptical wings, a long engine nose and a framed sliding canopy fits into 66,592 polygons. The first operational jet fighter, with swept wings and two underslung engines, spends 134,279 polygons on its triangular fuselage and glazed cockpit. A Cold War delta-wing interceptor keeps the nose intake with its shock cone and the pitot boom. An experimental jet shows forward-swept wings, canards and twin tails in 88,307 polygons.

Beyond complete airframes, a tandem cockpit of 119,180 polygons fills its consoles with switches, throttles, sticks and display bezels around two ejection seats. An afterburning turbofan from a fifth-generation fighter shows the casing, accessory gearbox and segmented nozzle petals in museum detail. Rigged models are rare. Among them is an animated scene of a short-takeoff stealth jet leaving an amphibious ship, with a swiveling rear nozzle and open lift fan doors.

Check the configuration before choosing. Some airframes are built in flight with the gear retracted, others stand on the ground, and a few simplified versions stay light for background traffic. CheckMate Pro certification here covers clean topology, consistent scale and a tidy scene. The fighters of the Aircraft category are aimed at aviation documentaries, museum and airshow displays, flight simulators, games and history lessons.

aircraft/airliners.lead: Passenger jets from compact regional twins to four-engine wide-bodies, plus a supersonic delta-wing airliner, converted freighters and military derivatives such as tankers, cargo lifters and patrol aircraft. Many airframes wear a generic livery. Complete passenger cabins, a forward fuselage cut behind the cockpit, landing gear parts and an airport taxiway scene complete the section.
body: A generic scheme is often more useful than an airline's own: it stands for commercial aviation in general and carries no brand that would date the image. The generic narrow-body twin is built that way in 278,966 polygons with 31 maps at 4096 x 4096. A long-haul twin wide-body at 757,593 polygons is judged on its raked wingtips, six-wheel main gear bogies, large nacelles and panel joins. For cruise shots, a narrow body in flight configuration has the gear retracted and flaps stowed. An aircraft with its gear down looks wrong at altitude.

Cabins are the heaviest work in the section. One narrow-body interior reaches 4,055,509 polygons, since every seat row, overhead bin, sidewall panel, window reveal and galley unit is built. A second cabin keeps seat stitching and tray tables sharp in 2,767,290 polygons. Smaller pieces suit maintenance training: a main gear wheel with its multi-disk brake pack exposed, and a forward fuselage section with frame rings open at the rear.

Most airliners are static, though an early four-engine jumbo with the upper deck hump is rigged, and a military cargo jet comes with its ramp lowered. CheckMate Pro certification on many models means real-world scale and clean topology. Airport visualization, travel advertising, aviation training, film and flight simulation are the usual destinations for these Aircraft models. One ground scene even shows a follow-me car guiding a trijet along the taxiway.

aircraft/drones.lead: Unmanned aircraft of every size: palm-sized nano helicopters, folding camera quadcopters with their controllers, fixed-wing survey drones, long-endurance surveillance aircraft, loitering munitions, carrier-based flying wings and passenger air taxi concepts. Ground equipment belongs here too, from a catapult launch rail to a vehicle-mounted counter-drone system with its radar and jammers.
body: Consumer and survey drones are modeled as products. A folding quadcopter of 66,437 polygons gives care to the gimbal, motor bells and arm hinges, with six maps for the gray shell, the lens and small printed markings. Another quadcopter comes with its smart controller, a handheld screen with twin joysticks, in subdivision-ready geometry. The mapping drone takes off vertically on twin nose rotors, then flies level to photograph fields, pipelines and building sites.

Military types are shown as hardware for documentaries, briefings and simulation. A catapult-launched reconnaissance drone small enough for two people to carry keeps its antennae, launch rail lugs and parachute hatch in 25,286 polygons. A tailless carrier flying wing sits with its wings folded, the way it spends most of its life on a crowded deck. The counter-drone system is exceptionally dense at 4,828,176 polygons, while a flying-wing loitering munition needs only 4,873.

Polygon budgets vary widely in this part of the Aircraft category, so match the model to the shot. Light builds such as an 11,347-polygon nano helicopter suit real-time scenes and games, while dense airframes hold up in close flybys. CheckMate Pro and StemCell certification appear across the section, and very few drones are rigged. A passenger multicopter with an enclosed cabin covers future city and urban air mobility scenes.

vehicles/trucks.lead: Trucks from pickups to long-haul tractors: crew-cab pickups, cab-over box trucks for city delivery, refuse and mail trucks, fire engines and semi tractors with box, reefer and tank trailers. An eight-wheel military cargo truck and a monster truck stand out. Engines, dual rear wheels, bare chassis and a doorless pickup body serve close-up and technical work.
body: A generic semi with trailer spends 724,720 polygons on a big rig that dominates a highway frame. Its fifth wheel, air lines, fuel tanks, mudflaps and ribbed box trailer are modeled rather than painted on. An electric semi tractor goes the other way, with no conventional grille or exhaust stack and a central driving position. On a conventional tractor the hood and grille are the face, so one long-nose model puts its chrome grille bars and sleeper cab into 260,918 polygons. A refuse truck builds the packer body, front loading arms and hopper, the parts that move and catch the light.

The technical shelf is unusually deep. A turbo diesel engine shows valve cover bolts, fuel lines, the exhaust manifold and belt-driven accessories. A bare heavy chassis waits to receive a body or crane, and a dual rear wheel assembly models every tread block and lug nut. One semi leaves its trailer sides blank for your own design or fleet branding. A touch-free car wash bay is rigged so the spray gantry travels around the pickup inside.

Many names include Simple Interior: the cab is there for windows and reflections, while the effort goes into the exterior. Simplified versions suit traffic and fleet scenes. Logistics and road visualization, driver training, advertising, film and games are the natural uses, and trailers on their own have a neighboring section in the Vehicles category.

vehicles/trailers.lead: Trailers of every hitch and purpose: box and refrigerated semi trailers, tankers for liquids and liquefied gas, flatbeds, lowboys and extendable heavy-haul decks. Small utility, boat, motorcycle and agricultural dump trailers are here too. Several tractor-and-trailer combinations, a bare trailer chassis and a surge brake actuator cover scenes that need the full rig or a single part.
body: A tanker is judged by its hardware. The tanker semi trailer puts its 511,203 polygons into the ribbed barrel, the top walkway and handrail, the manhole lids and the valve cabinet at the rear. Its 35 texture maps cover the polished and painted shell. The liquefied gas trailer looks nothing like it: a vacuum-insulated pressure vessel with domed ends and a smooth shell without visible ribs. The flatbed, the oldest trailer type still in wide use, puts no limit on the shape of the load.

For heavy haulage, a double drop lowboy sets its deck between a raised gooseneck and a rear axle group. An extendable trailer slides out to carry beams, blades or pipes, and a loaded flatbed carries strapped-down crates in 2,460,585 polygons. Smaller pieces are modeled just as carefully. The boat trailer is all quads, with a galvanized frame, padded bunks and a winch post, so welds and leaf springs hold up close.

Decide between standalone trailers and complete rigs: the generic semi, a yard tractor with its lifting fifth wheel and several long-nose tractors come already hitched. A brake actuator of 29,896 polygons shows the coupler latch and fluid reservoir for towing explainers. Ports and logistics yards, depots, farms, driver training and games all draw on this Vehicles section.

vehicles/suvs.lead: Sport utility vehicles from compact crossovers to full-size family haulers and boxy luxury off-roaders, most of them generic and unbadged. There are electric and premium crossovers, dirty and simplified versions for background traffic, and an unusual technical shelf: bare ladder frames, chassis and front suspension assemblies shown without any body panels.
body: A generic SUV can serve a client better than a branded one. No badge means no licensing question, no dating of the image and no client asking why a competitor's car is parked outside. The heaviest of them reaches 1,014,361 polygons, with the engine bay, cabin, door cards, dash and undercarriage all built. A boxy luxury off-roader keeps its upright glass, round headlights, side-exit exhaust and the spare wheel on the tailgate. A black premium crossover has a full-length panoramic roof, so a high camera sees into the cabin and aerial city shots gain life.

Several pages answer practical needs. An SUV with a compact camping trailer has the coupling placed correctly at the drawbar, so the pair can be animated turning or reversing without the trailer drifting off. A fabric cover draped over an SUV describes its folds around the mirrors and wheel arches in only 22,709 polygons. The chassis frames show rails, crossmembers, coil springs, brake discs and steering linkage for engineering and repair visuals.

With SUVs, as elsewhere in the Vehicles category, decide first how close the camera goes. Full interiors suit close-ups, simple interiors fill parking lots, and dirty or simplified builds sit in the background. Expect to see these SUVs on driveways in architectural renders, at hotel arrivals, in automotive advertising and in workshop training.

vehicles/buses.lead: Buses for city, school and long-distance scenes: red London double-deckers, low-floor and articulated transit buses, yellow American school buses, charter coaches, an open-top sightseeing bus and driverless electric shuttles. Period and story pieces round it out, from a seventies intercity coach and a streamlined railway coach car to a prison transport bus with an officer and an inmate.
body: The classic London double-decker carries 132 texture maps at 8192 x 8192 and 4096 x 4096. Signage, livery, interior fabric and advertising panels each need their own resolution, while the interior is simplified for a bus seen from the street. An articulated city bus of 639,920 polygons builds the bellows joint as real geometry, since the bus bends through junctions. A driverless electric shuttle uses the symmetrical pod shape with no front or back, sensor and lidar housings on the roof and bench seating behind the glass.

School buses follow rules that make them recognizable in silhouette. The yellow is regulated, chosen as the most visible thing on a road at dawn, and the black rub rails, stop arm, crossing gate and flashing lights are mandated too. Any deviation looks wrong, so these models keep every one of them. A low-floor North American transit bus adds the wheelchair ramp, roof hatches, bike rack mounts and articulated door panels.

Most buses come with a simple or basic interior. One two-door electric city bus arrives without texture maps, leaving paint and glass to your own materials, which suits a custom transit livery. A London set pairs the double-decker with a black cab, and an older American city bus is rigged. Street visualization, transit planning, period film and bus advertising mockups lean on these Vehicles models.

vehicles/motorcycles.lead: Two-wheelers and their relatives: V-twin cruisers, naked street bikes, sportbikes, a vintage Italian tourer, maxi scooters, electric scooters and mopeds, and motocross bikes. Riders appear on a superbike and a junior dirt bike. Stranger machines such as a white monowheel and a sci-fi bike sit beside loose wheels, a stripped engine and frame, and trailers built to haul bikes.
body: A cruiser is defined by its stance, and the 288,010-polygon cruiser keeps it: a low seat, forward controls, a wide rear tire and the V-twin left visible between the frame tubes. A small-capacity naked bike with a short wheelbase and high bars carries 13 maps, nine of them at 8192 x 8192. A naked hypersport machine goes to 1,059,721 polygons for its brake discs, chain links, radiator fins and stitched seat. The generic street motorcycle, with a teardrop tank and round headlight, copies no single manufacturer, so it can stand in any city scene without questions about the design.

Parts are useful on their own. A motocross rear wheel models the laced spokes, knobby tread and sprocket in 34,246 polygons, and a road front wheel with a drilled rotor suits custom builds and cafe racers. A motocross engine and frame stripped of plastics shows the single-cylinder motor, swingarm, cooling fins and welded tubes. For transport scenes there are a folding single-rail trailer carrying a dirt bike, a three-place track trailer and a small folding trailer that hitches behind a touring bike.

Expect static models here rather than rigged ones. Automotive advertising, garage and showroom renders, racing and city games, and film are the obvious homes for this Vehicles subcategory. Lighter scooters and the self-balancing personal transporter suit urban mobility scenes, while the sci-fi bike with hubless wheels catches neon reflections in rainy night streets.

medical-3d-models/human-anatomy.lead: Anatomy models for teaching and medical explanation: full-body figures with skin and organs, heads and limbs built layer by layer, and single organs such as the brain, eye, ear, lungs and urinary tract. Smaller pieces include a nerve cell, knee and shoulder joints, breast cutaways and a skin block on a stand.
body: A head with both anatomy and skin is two assets in one: the face gives context, and the muscles, bones and vessels beneath it carry the explanation. Fading between them only works when the skin sits correctly over the structures, and this head uses 312 texture maps to keep each part distinct. The skinless head and neck takes the same approach with 311 maps, so a muscle group, vessel or gland can be isolated and labeled instead of lit as one red mass. The leg with skin answers why the surface looks the way it does: the hollow behind the knee and the line down the shin follow from what sits underneath.

Other models are light by design. The muscular system without a skeleton runs on 7,408 polygons and shows origins and insertions clearly. The lungs use 15,902 polygons and five maps, enough for browser lessons, and they keep the left lung with two lobes rather than three. A nerve cell needs only 2,429 polygons, and a pregnancy breast model is built from 946 for mobile courseware. The sectioned eye shows the lens behind the iris, the vitreous, the retina and the optic nerve.

Within the Medical category, choose by layers and weight: skin with anatomy for fades, skinless models for muscle work, single organs for focused lessons. A knee model is prepared for 3D printing, with the bones as solid pieces. Typical users are medical schools, patient education, explainer animation and interactive courseware.

medical-3d-models/skeleton-bones.lead: Skeletons and bones for anatomy teaching, orthopedics, forensic and story scenes: complete male and female skeletons, torsos, ribcages, pelvises, arms, legs, hands, feet and knees, and a skull that comes apart. Some figures add organs, vessels and nerves to the bones. Surgical pieces sit alongside, such as skull clamps, a bone saw and a cranial mesh implant.
body: In a skeleton the proportion carries the anatomy. The complete female skeleton makes every bone a separate object, so the ribs can be separated, the pelvis isolated and the vertebrae counted, with 27 maps across 80,733 polygons. The full male skeleton keeps each vertebra, rib and finger joint distinct and carries 75 maps at 8192 x 8192 and 4096 x 4096, an unusually rich set for bone. A skeleton with internal organs shows the ribcage over the lungs and heart and the pelvis around the lower organs. That pairing of layers teaches spatial relationships most clearly.

Regional models stay light for web viewers and apps. The hand bones need 3,958 polygons, the leg bones from hip to toes 8,186, and the foot skeleton holds its natural arch in 15,065. A hand skeleton with the flexor retinaculum shows the roof of the carpal tunnel, and the female pelvis spends its 4,960 polygons on the oval inlet and the flared iliac wings. The disassemblable skull lifts off its cap and lower jaw to reveal the inner surface of the vault.

Surgical and story pieces broaden the use. A three-pin skull clamp reaches 7,569,760 polygons, a display skull shows a mesh implant closing a defect, and a shackled skeleton slumped against a wall dresses a dungeon. Anatomy classes, orthopedic and physiotherapy explainers, forensic scenes and patient communication make up most of the work for this Medical subcategory.

medical-3d-models/dental.lead: Dental models for clinics, schools and patient explanation: teeth and jaws, typodonts with removable or transparent parts, braces, retainers and implants. The equipment of a dental office is here as well, from the chair and a panoramic X-ray unit to drills, forceps, mirrors and a dental 3D printer. Everyday oral care items such as floss and toothbrush sets round it out.
body: Dental work is judged at the scale of a millimeter. A clear retainer of 17,484 polygons is nothing but its molding, a transparent shell that follows the contour of each tooth. That shell is what makes it read as orthodontic rather than as a mouthguard. The dental handpiece keeps the angled head, bur, water ports and ribbed grip, with three maps for polished steel, the matte grip and the engraving on the collar. A tooth in cross section separates enamel, dentin, pulp chamber and root canals, and the dental mold shapes every crown individually along the cusps and gum line.

Typodonts form a group of their own. Transparent versions show implants inside the jawbone, while a pediatric typodont with removable overbite teeth lets orthodontic and restorative steps be shown one at a time. Teeth with metal brackets and an archwire spend most of their 33,856 polygons on brackets and ligatures. A lower jaw with an implant explains why the screw works, titanium bonding to bone, in 8,995 polygons light enough for interactive material.

For the office itself, the dental chair carries an overhead light, an instrument tray on an articulated arm and a spittoon unit. The X-ray unit circles the head on a rotating arm. A braces model prepared as one closed shape suits resin or filament 3D printing. Clinic websites, patient explanations, dental school lessons and product renders are where these Medical models do their work.

medical-3d-models/medical-equipment.lead: The working equipment of clinics and hospitals: disposable syringes in several volumes, manual, powered and vintage wheelchairs, and MRI, CT and ultrasound scanners. A vital signs monitor, a crash cart, a stretcher trolley, kidney dishes and bulb syringes fill out the wards. A few neighbors from related fields land here too, including firefighter breathing apparatus and school chemistry labs.
body: Small details decide whether a prop reads as clinical. A syringe is a measuring instrument, so the 2 ml set models the barrel graduations, flange, plunger seal and needle hub. A plain barrel would look like a toy. A lighter syringe of 3,126 polygons lets dozens fill a tray or a sharps container. The powered wheelchair is built as its own object rather than a manual chair with a motor. It has a molded seat on a powered base, front casters, mid drive wheels, a joystick on the armrest and a battery under the seat.

Imaging equipment covers several budgets. The MRI scanner puts its detail into the bore mouth, the sliding table and the cable runs, while a CT scanner of only 12,087 polygons suits real-time scenes. A cart-based ultrasound system adds a tilting monitor, a trackball and holstered probes. The crash cart carries a defibrillator shelf and 13 maps for powder-coated steel, plastic trim and labels. The stretcher trolley with an infusion stand stays light enough to line a corridor.

For hospital interiors in architectural visualization, medical simulation, healthcare advertising and documentaries, this Medical subcategory covers the rooms from corridor to scanner. The chemistry classroom scenes are better read as school interiors, with benches, fume hoods and shelves of glassware.

animals-creatures/dogs.lead: Dogs by breed and by pose: pugs, Jack Russell terriers, boxers, bulldogs, Labrador puppies, a husky and Dalmatians, plus cartoon puppies for children's animation. The section also covers veterinary anatomy, with skulls, jaws, teeth, a spine and full skeletons, and everyday pet scenes such as a bulldog asleep in its bed or a puppy at the food bowl.
body: Most breeds come in more than one form. A Jack Russell terrier stands in an attention pose, ears perked and head raised as if waiting for a command, in 16,134 polygons, and another version carries spotted fur. The pug is offered whole and as a separate head that spends its polygons on the deep facial folds. A boxer sits upright with a square jaw and wrinkled brow, and the bulldog fur version keeps a light base body of 12,131 polygons under groomed strands. Dalmatians are rigged and animated with fur, running, walking and sitting, the walk a level-headed trot.

Scenes add a story to the animal. A Labrador puppy sits beside an accident on a doormat, and since puppy, mat and mess are separate objects, the joke can be removed. A brown Labrador braces its paws around a food bowl, the familiar pet food shot, and a husky wears a nylon muzzle. A terrier and a cartoon puppy wear collar tracker tags for pet tech stories, and a robot dog walks beside a humanoid robot.

Veterinary pieces round out the dog pages of Animals & Creatures. A skeleton under a translucent body shell shows where each joint sits under the coat, while skulls, jaws and a spine suit lectures. The cartoon puppy runs on 4,346 polygons for mobile games, and the realistic dogs suit pet supply advertising, family animation and home interiors.

animals-creatures/fish-marine.lead: Sharks, whales, dolphins, reef fish and food fish: a great white, a hammerhead, tiger and reef sharks, a humpback whale, salmon, tuna, herring, koi, sturgeon, parrotfish and a common octopus. The section also holds shark jaws and fossil teeth for natural history, and fish as food, from a tuna on a cleaning board to cod on ice in a display case.
body: Fish move in shoals, so many models in this Animals & Creatures subcategory are deliberately light. The Atlantic salmon uses 3,930 polygons and lets the body taper, the adipose fin and the jaw line carry the species, while five maps hold the scales and the silver sheen along the flank. The rigged bottlenose dolphin stays at 11,362 polygons because the form is simple and the rig matters more: a dolphin is interesting in motion. The tiger shark keeps its vertical bars in the texture rather than the mesh, since those markings fade with age.

Natural history pieces go into fine detail. A great white jaw in quads builds every tooth individually, including the replacement rows behind the front ones, the arrangement that makes it unmistakably a shark. A fossil tooth of an extinct shark keeps its serrated edges, the small cusplets at the root and the mineral staining in only 1,511 polygons. The octopus follows every arm taper and sucker row in 55,991 polygons for macro shots.

For schools and reefs, the hammerhead, herring and parrotfish duplicate easily, and an animated salmon swims in a loop. Food scenes include a dorado with a crab in its jaws and a mackerel lying on deck. From aquariums and nature documentaries to marine biology lessons and seafood advertising, the section covers both the living animal and the catch on ice.

animals-creatures/birds.lead: Birds of prey, owls, waders and farmyard poultry: bald, golden, imperial and Gurney's eagles in several poses, barn, great horned and snowy owls, gray and blue herons, hens and a coop with its flock. Loose feathers, a single eagle feather, songbirds at a birdbath and a bird skull beside a candle extend the section beyond whole birds.
body: Raptors are where the texture work concentrates. The imperial eagle carries 44 maps on 33,039 polygons, because each feather group has its own direction, gloss and edge wear that one map cannot hold. The Gurney's eagle follows suit with 43 maps, and its CheckMate Pro certification guarantees real-world scale. That matters, since wingspan is what makes an eagle read as an eagle. The golden eagle layers individual flight feathers along each wing, and the barn owl keeps its heart-shaped facial disc and feathered legs.

Animated birds show what a still pose cannot. A rigged chicken is set up for the motion that matters: the head stays still while the body moves, the detail that separates a believable hen from a toy. A snowy owl lands with wings flared and, in a second version, idles on a perch while turning its head and blinking. A gray heron flies with its neck tucked and legs stretched behind, beating slow, deep wingbeats.

Feathers get pages of their own within Animals & Creatures: a set of loose plumes from stiff flight feathers to downy tufts reaches 417,384 polygons to model individual barbs. The eagles suit wildlife and heraldic scenes, and the hens and red coop suit farm and food origin imagery. Owls and herons work for documentaries, games and nature lessons.

animals-creatures/insects.lead: Insects and spiders for macro shots and nature lessons: monarch, morpho, peacock, red admiral, swallowtail and birdwing butterflies and an owl moth. Honey bees, a red ant, a dragonfly, a praying mantis, potato beetles and a stick insect follow. Arachnids include garden, house and mouse spiders and a camel spider, with a chrysalis and an insect in amber at the edges.
body: Butterflies are judged by their wings, so the pattern has to be exact. The monarch keeps its orange panels divided by heavy black veins and the black border with two rows of white spots, a warning signal rather than decoration. The blue morpho poses a material problem rather than a texture one: its blue is structural color and shifts toward near black as the viewing angle changes. The birdwing, the largest butterfly in the world, carries StemCell PBR materials so its iridescence survives in a real-time engine. The peacock butterfly uses seven texture sheets down to the blue scales inside each eyespot.
